l12_1_objective: A model writes one token at a time: it scores every possible next token, picks one, adds it to the text and repeats — until it picks a special “end” token.
l12_1_misconception: The model plans the whole answer first, then types it out.
l12_1_intro: These are real recordings: we ran a small open model (Qwen2.5, half a billion parameters) and saved the 5 most likely candidates it saw at every step. Walk through them and predict what it does next.
l12_1_r1_prompt: The text so far: “Once upon a time, a little”. Which next token did the model rate highest?
l12_1_r1_explain: “boy” at 36.6% — but “girl” was right behind at 34.0%. The model doesn't know one right word; it gives a probability to every token it knows. In this recording it always takes the top one, so a 2.6-point gap decided the whole story.
l12_1_r2_prompt: The model has written “… a little boy named Tim”. Now it gives “my” 93.3%. What does that tell you?
l12_1_r2_opt0: Tokens are pieces, not words: “Tim” + “my” makes the name “Timmy”.
l12_1_r2_opt2: “my” is simply the most common word in English.
l12_1_r2_explain: “Tim” only got 6.9% one step earlier, but once it was written, “my” became almost certain (93.3%): the model is finishing the name “Timmy”. In the last round the chat reply spells “captivates” as three tokens — “capt”, “iv”, “ates”. One word is often several tokens.
l12_1_r3_prompt: The story now reads “… playing with his toy”. How sure is the model about the next token?
l12_1_r3_opt0: Very sure — there is one right answer.
l12_1_r3_opt1: Not very: even its favourite gets only about a quarter of the probability.
l12_1_r3_opt2: Not at all — it is typing random letters.
l12_1_r3_explain: “car” leads with only 26.9%, then “box”, “train”, “boat”… Many continuations make sense, and the leftover probability is spread across thousands of other tokens. Compare “with” in the chat reply: 100.0%. Confidence changes from step to step.
l12_1_r4_prompt: Now a chat model answers “Describe the sea in one short sentence.” with the same loop. After “… captivates the imagination.” the reply stops. Why?
l12_1_r4_opt0: The app cuts every reply off after 24 tokens.
l12_1_r4_opt1: A sentence ended, and models always stop at a full stop.
l12_1_r4_opt2: The model predicted a special “end of reply” token — stopping is a prediction too.
l12_1_r4_explain: Step 24 is the end-of-reply token at 100.0%. Chat models are trained to produce it when an answer is complete, and the app stops the loop when it appears. At every step of this lesson the model took its top choice — real chat apps often don't, and the next module shows why.
l12_1_hint1: Read the bars: the longest one is the model's favourite next token.
l12_1_hint2: A token can be part of a word. Glue the chosen tokens together and see what you get.
l12_1_hint3: Nothing outside the model ends the reply — look at what the very last bar says.
l12_2_objective: Inside a model, every token becomes a long list of numbers (an embedding). Words with similar meanings get similar numbers — even across languages.
l12_2_misconception: A model stores words as text and looks them up like a dictionary.
l12_2_intro: We gave 40 words — the same 8 meanings in English, Turkish, Spanish, French and Chinese — to a real embedding model (EmbeddingGemma) and measured how alike each pair is: 1.00 means pointing the same way, lower means less alike.
l12_2_r1_prompt: “kedi” is Turkish for cat. Which of these did the model place closest to it?
l12_2_r1_explain: “gato” (Spanish for cat) at 0.88 — closer than “köpek” (dog, 0.79), even though köpek is Turkish too. The model groups by meaning, not by language. Cats and dogs still sit near each other: both are pets.
l12_2_r2_prompt: “国王” is Chinese for king. Which of these is closest to it?
l12_2_r2_explain: “king” at 0.92 — a different alphabet, the same place on the map. “狗” (dog) shares the script but sits at 0.63. Letters don't decide closeness; meaning does.
l12_2_r3_prompt: Look at “araba” (Turkish for car) and its nearest neighbours. What does closeness on this map measure?
l12_2_r3_opt1: How similar the meaning is — usually right, but not perfect.
l12_2_r3_explain: For 39 of the 40 words, the nearest neighbour is a translation. “araba” is the exception: its nearest is “elma” (apple, 0.74), just ahead of “coche” (0.72) and “car” (0.72). Embeddings capture meaning well, but they are measurements, not definitions.
l12_2_hint1: Spelling and alphabet don't matter here — think about what the words mean.
l12_2_hint2: Translations of the same word tend to land close together.
l12_2_hint3: After answering, click any word: the lines always show its real nearest neighbours.
l12_3_objective: To predict each token, a model weighs every earlier token and pulls in the ones that matter — even from far back. This is called attention.
l12_3_misconception: A model only looks at the last few words.
l12_3_intro: Same small model, real recordings. We can't open its attention weights directly (this model file doesn't expose them), so we measure the behaviour instead: change or delete one early word and watch the prediction at the very end.
l12_3_copy_a: Story A — keys in the drawer
l12_3_copy_b: Story B — keys in the basket
l12_3_r1_prompt: The two stories differ in one word near the start (highlighted). A long stretch about tea, emails and plants sits between it and the end. What does the model predict as the last word?
l12_3_r1_opt0: “drawer” in both — it's the more common word.
l12_3_r1_opt1: “drawer” in A and “basket” in B — it looks back to the start.
l12_3_r1_opt2: A word from the nearby middle part, like “book”, in both.
l12_3_r1_explain: Story A: “drawer” 90.8%. Story B: “basket” 99.9% — and “drawer” falls to almost 0. Dozens of tokens separate that first mention from the end, and the model still pulls it back in. Copying from earlier in the text like this is one of the most reliable things attention does.
l12_3_r2_prompt: In a shorter version, we deleted the words one at a time and measured how much the chance of “drawer” at the end dropped. Which deletion hurt it most?
l12_3_r2_explain: Deleting “drawer” takes it from 95.6% to 1.1%; deleting either “blue” costs about 84 points. Deleting “Ayla” barely matters (0.9 points). The heat map is measured, not drawn: it shows which words the prediction really depends on.
l12_3_r3_prompt: Both sentences contain “mouse”, but the earlier words tell the model which mouse it is. Do the predictions at the end differ?
l12_3_r3_opt0: No — “mouse” is one word with one meaning.
l12_3_r3_opt1: Yes — the earlier words decide which “mouse” it is, and the predictions follow.
l12_3_r3_explain: Computer mouse: “on” leads with 36.8% (“clicked on…”), and “ran” gets almost nothing. The cat's mouse: “was” 29.5% and “ran” 5.6%, while “on” drops to almost nothing. Attention lets the same word carry a different meaning in each context.
l12_3_hint1: Find the single highlighted word that differs between the two stories.
l12_3_hint2: The model can reach back across a whole paragraph — distance doesn't stop it.
l12_3_hint3: Ask which word the last word is really copying.
l13_1_objective: Training happens in stages: first a model learns to continue text from a huge pile of documents; then it is trained on example conversations — and on which answers people prefer — to become an assistant.
l13_1_misconception: A chat model was built to answer questions from the very beginning.
l13_1_intro: Two real models from the same family, same size: Qwen2.5-0.5B is the raw “base” model, trained only to continue text; Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct is the same model after chat training. Same request to both; replies capped at 50 tokens.
l13_1_r1_prompt: You type “I feel a bit sad today.” What does the base model write?
l13_1_r1_opt1: It carries on as if it had written your sentence itself.
l13_1_r1_explain: The base model writes “I feel a bit sad because I have been away from my family…” and then repeats itself. It has only learned to continue documents, so your message is just the first line of someone's diary. The chat model replies to you: “I'm sorry to hear that…”.
l13_1_r2_prompt: Now “What should I cook for dinner tonight?”. What does the base model do?
l13_1_r2_opt2: Turns it into a multiple-choice quiz, like a dataset it once read.
l13_1_r2_explain: It repeats the question and adds “Multi-choice problem: Are these two questions inquiring about the same information?”. Pages like that were in its training text, so that is a likely continuation. The chat model suggests dishes.
l13_1_r3_prompt: “Tell me a joke.” This time the base model does tell one. If it was never trained to answer, why does it look like an answer?
l13_1_r3_opt0: It is secretly a chat model.
l13_1_r3_opt1: On the web, a line like “Tell me a joke.” is usually followed by a joke — it's continuing a familiar pattern.
l13_1_r3_explain: “Why did the chicken cross the road? To get to the other side!” — the most familiar joke there is. Lots of web text is a question followed by its answer, so a base model often looks helpful. It is still only continuing text; chat training makes answering the reliable default.
l13_1_r4_prompt: Which order matches how chat models are made?
l13_1_r4_opt0: 1) Predict the next token across a huge pile of text → 2) train on example conversations → 3) train on which answers people prefer.
l13_1_r4_opt1: 1) Train on conversations → 2) add facts from a database → 3) connect it to the internet.
l13_1_r4_opt2: Engineers write the rules for every answer by hand.
l13_1_r4_explain: Stage 1 (pre-training) is where almost all of the knowledge comes from, and it takes by far the most computing. Stage 2 teaches the shape of a conversation. Stage 3 nudges the model toward answers people rate as better: more helpful, more honest, safer. No stage adds a database or a live internet connection.
l13_1_hint1: The base model has never seen a conversation format — only documents.
l13_1_hint2: Ask yourself: on a web page, what usually comes right after this line?
l13_1_hint3: Knowledge comes first, from raw text; the conversation manners come afterwards.
l13_2_objective: A model always writes the likeliest-sounding continuation, so it can state made-up facts in a confident tone (hallucination). And it knows nothing after its training data ends (its knowledge cutoff).
l13_2_misconception: If the model sounds sure, it must know.
l13_2_intro: Real replies from the chat model of the previous lesson (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct). None of these countries exist, and the 2030 World Cup has not been played.
l13_2_r1_prompt: We asked for the capital of 10 made-up countries. How many times did the model say it doesn't know?
l13_2_r1_explain: Only 2. For the other 8 it invented an answer — “Zarnovo”, “Brindledale”, “Kelmoria City” — in the same calm tone it uses for real facts. One reply even describes Quessary as “a fictional world in Chinese science fiction”. Tone tells you nothing about truth.
l13_2_r2_prompt: “Who won the 2030 FIFA World Cup final?” What did the model reply?
l13_2_r2_opt0: It said the tournament hasn't happened yet.
l13_2_r2_opt1: After a disclaimer, it said Argentina beat Germany on 14 September 2030.
l13_2_r2_opt2: It said it doesn't know and stopped.
l13_2_r2_explain: It opens with “As an artificial intelligence language model…” and then invents a final, a winner and a date. Its training text ended years before 2030, so the result cannot be in it — but a confident-sounding answer is still the likeliest continuation.
l13_2_r3_prompt: Why does a model invent an answer instead of saying “I don't know”?
l13_2_r3_opt1: It looked something up in a database with wrong entries.
l13_2_r3_opt2: It writes the likeliest continuation; “The capital of X is Y” is a very common pattern, while “I don't know” only becomes likely if training rewarded it.
l13_2_r3_explain: There is no table of facts inside, only next-token probabilities. Newer models are trained to say “I don't know” more often and can check sources with tools, which reduces hallucination — but no model is immune. Double-check anything that matters.
l13_2_r4_prompt: Claude Opus 5.5's training data ends in June 2026 (its knowledge cutoff). Without any tools, you ask it about an event from August 2026. What happens?
l13_2_r4_opt0: It can't know. It may say so — or make something up. Given a tool like web search, it could read a current page instead.
l13_2_r4_opt1: It knows — models are always connected to the internet.
l13_2_r4_opt2: It knows — models are retrained every night.
l13_2_r4_explain: A model is frozen when training ends. Chat apps often cover for this by giving it tools such as web search, or by putting today's date in the prompt — but the model itself learns nothing new after its cutoff. Each model has its own cutoff; GPT-6 Astra's is 30 April 2026.
l13_2_hint1: Count the replies that say “I'm sorry” or “I don't have”.
l13_2_hint2: There is no list of facts inside a model — only probabilities for the next token.
l13_2_hint3: A model can't read about events that happened after its training data was collected.
l14_1_objective: Reasoning models write hidden “thinking” tokens before they answer. That often fixes mistakes, it costs extra output tokens, and it is not magic.
l14_1_misconception: A thinking model reasons like a person, so its answers are always right.
l14_1_intro: A real small reasoning model (Qwen3, 0.6 billion parameters) whose thinking can be switched on or off. We asked each question 3 times per mode, with random sampling and fixed seeds.
l14_1_r1_prompt: “Is 91 a prime number?” (It isn't: 91 = 7 × 13.) How did the model do with thinking off and on?
l14_1_r1_explain: Without thinking it answered “Yes” all 3 times, in 10–16 tokens. With thinking it first wrote 221 to 365 hidden tokens — trying 2, 3 and 5, then finding 7 × 13 — and answered “No” all 3 times. Same model, same weights: writing out the steps made the difference.
l14_1_r2_prompt: “How many times does the letter r appear in strawberry?” (Answer: 3.) What happened with thinking on?
l14_1_r2_opt2: 0/3 right — it spelled S-T-R-A-W-B-E-R-R-Y correctly while thinking, then still answered 2.
l14_1_r2_explain: All 3 thinking runs spelled the word out letter by letter (161 to 204 hidden tokens each) and still concluded 2; thinking off got it right once. The model never sees letters — the question reaches it as tokens like “str”, “aw”, “berry”. Thinking helps with steps, not with what the model can't see.
l14_1_r3_prompt: On real hosted models, how are those hidden thinking tokens handled?
l14_1_r3_opt0: They're free — only the visible answer is billed.
l14_1_r3_opt1: They're billed as output tokens and usually hidden from you; on some models, such as Claude Opus 5.5, thinking can't be switched off — you can only set how much effort it spends.
l14_1_r3_explain: Thinking is text the model writes, so it is billed as output — often more tokens than the answer itself. Many providers show you a summary, or nothing, instead of the raw thoughts, and you pay for them either way.
l14_1_hint1: Compare the ✓ and ✗ marks in the two columns.
l14_1_hint2: Thinking is extra text the model writes before answering — and text is tokens.
l14_1_hint3: Open a hidden thought: does the model spell the word right? Does it count right?
l14_2_objective: A vision model cuts an image into small squares, and each square is one token — counted like text in the context window and on the bill. Bigger images cost more, up to a limit; beyond it they are shrunk first.
l14_2_misconception: Images are free — only the text of a message counts.
l14_2_intro: Pick an image size and see the grid the model actually reads. The numbers follow the published rules for current Claude models.
l14_2_r1_explain: 200 ÷ 28 rounds up to 8, so the grid is 8 × 8 = 64 tokens. 40,000 is the number of pixels — the model doesn't pay per pixel, it pays per 28 × 28 square.
l14_2_r2_prompt: A 12-megapixel phone photo, 4032 × 3024. How many tokens does the model see?
l14_2_r2_explain: At full size it would be 144 × 108 = 15,552 tokens, over the limit of 4,784 per image. So the photo is first shrunk to 2212 × 1659: 79 × 60 = 4,740 tokens. A giant photo buys no extra detail beyond the limit.
l14_2_r3_prompt: A 1920 × 1080 screenshot costs 2,691 tokens. What does that mean for you?
l14_2_r3_opt0: Nothing — images don't count toward the context window.
l14_2_r3_opt1: It takes up room in the context window and is billed as input, just like text — a few screenshots can outweigh a long message.
l14_2_r3_opt2: Only the file size in megabytes matters.
l14_2_r3_explain: Visual tokens live in the same context window and on the same bill as text. At Claude Opus 5.5's input price of $4 per million tokens, that screenshot costs about a cent — cheap once, but an agent that takes a screenshot at every step adds up fast.
l14_2_hint1: Divide each side by 28 and round up — that's the grid.
l14_2_hint2: Very large images are shrunk until they fit the token limit.
l14_2_hint3: A screenshot sits in the same window as your words.
